title: Benford's Law: Why Does the Digit 1 Lead So Often?
question: Why do the first digits of real-world numbers favor 1 over 9, and what does that reveal about how numbers arise in nature?
summary: In populations, river lengths, stock prices and electricity bills, about 30% of numbers begin with 1 and under 5% with 9. The pattern is a signature of scale-free processes, and it has caught fraudsters.
content:
Open a table of country populations, the lengths of the world's rivers, or the numbers on a company's invoices, and count the leading digits. Intuition says each of 1 through 9 should appear about 11% of the time. Reality says otherwise: 1 leads roughly 30% of the time, 2 about 18%, and 9 fewer than 5%. This is Benford's law, noticed by astronomer Simon Newcomb in 1881 when he saw that the early pages of logarithm tables were more worn than the later ones, and rediscovered by physicist Frank Benford in 1938.

The Law Itself

The probability that a number begins with digit d is log10(1 + 1/d). That is a strangely specific formula, and it hints at the cause: logarithms. Numbers that grow multiplicatively spend as long getting from 1,000 to 2,000 (doubling) as from 2,000 to 4,000, but only a fraction of that from 8,000 to 9,000. On a logarithmic ruler, the stretch of "numbers starting with 1" is simply the longest.

Why Scale Invariance Forces It

Suppose a dataset has a universal first-digit distribution that does not depend on the units used. Whether you measure in dollars or euros, metres or feet, the leading-digit frequencies should not change, since the choice of unit is arbitrary. Ted Hill proved in 1995 that the only distribution satisfying this scale invariance (together with base invariance) is Benford's. In other words, the law is what "no preferred unit" looks like in digits.

Where It Appears, and Where It Fails

It shows up in data that spans several orders of magnitude and arises from multiplicative growth or mixtures of many sources: city sizes, physical constants, Fibonacci numbers, powers of 2. It fails for data with a narrow range (adult heights in centimetres), assigned numbers (phone numbers, lottery draws) or imposed bounds (prices set at $9.99 clustering at 9). The failures are as informative as the successes: they tell you the data was not generated by a scale-free process.

A Forensic Tool

People inventing numbers tend to spread digits evenly, because that feels random. Auditors exploit this. Mark Nigrini popularized Benford tests for tax returns and accounting data, and statisticians have applied similar checks to election returns and to reported data in scientific papers. A deviation is not proof of fraud, but it is a reason to look closer.

perspectives.title: Mathematical
perspectives.description: The law follows from scale and base invariance (Hill's theorem), and from the fact that the logarithm of a multiplicatively growing quantity is roughly uniformly distributed modulo 1.

perspectives.title: Physical
perspectives.description: Many natural quantities are products of many independent factors. By the central limit theorem applied to logs, such products are approximately log-normal and spread widely enough to yield Benford digits.

perspectives.title: Forensic Accounting
perspectives.description: Humans are poor random-number generators. Comparing digit frequencies against Benford's law offers a cheap first-pass screen for fabricated financial data.

perspectives.title: Philosophical
perspectives.description: A pattern that depends on nothing but the absence of a preferred unit suggests some regularities are statements about our description of the world rather than about the world itself.

openQuestions: Why do so many diverse real datasets approximate Benford's law without any obvious multiplicative mechanism?
How can forensic Benford tests be made robust against fraudsters who know the law?
Is there a deeper link between Benford's law, Zipf's law and other power-law regularities?
Can deviations from Benford's law be quantified in a way that supports legal standards of evidence?
